s03-startup.text: Look outside the window! Is it sunny, cloudy, or rainy? Have you ever noticed how the weather changes throughout the day? Some places are always warm, while others are cold.
Why does this happen? In this chapter, we will explore the differences between weather and climate and understand the factors that influence them.

s04-weather.text: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a particular place and time. It includes temperature, wind, rainfall, humidity, and cloud cover.
Weather can change from hour to hour or day to day. For example, one morning, it may be sunny and by afternoon it could rain.

s06-climate.text: Climate is the average weather condition of a place over a long period, usually 30 years or more. It tells us whether a place is generally hot, cold, wet, or dry.
For example, the climate of the Sahara Desert is hot and dry, while the climate of the Amazon Rainforest is warm and rainy.

s08-latitude.text: The Earth is divided into imaginary lines called latitudes. Places near the equator receive direct sunlight throughout the year, making them hot.
As we move towards the poles, sunlight spreads out, making these areas cooler. This is why tropical regions are warm, while polar regions are cold.

s10-sea-land-breeze.text: Oceans and seas influence the climate of coastal areas. Water heats up and cools down more slowly than land.
During the day, land heats up faster than water, causing a sea breeze to blow from the sea to the land.
At night, the land cools down quickly, and a land breeze blows from land to the sea. This keeps coastal areas cooler in summer and warmer in winter compared to inland regions.

s13-currents.text: Ocean currents are large movements of water in the oceans. Warm ocean currents make coastal areas warmer, while cold currents bring cool temperatures.
For example, the Gulf Stream warms Europe, while the cold Labrador Current cools Canada.

s26-recall.text: Weather and climate are essential aspects of our environment. Many factors, such as latitude, altitude, wind, and ocean currents, influence climate.
Different regions experience different types of climates, affecting the way people live, the food they grow and the clothes they wear.
